Empirical Research Plan: Hedge-Fund Shareholder Activism (2001–2006)

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
I use a two-pronged approach:

A. Event-study (market model) around the first public activism signal (initial Schedule 13D filing) to identify the short-run stock-price reaction that capital markets impute to activism.  
B. Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with staggered treatment timing to estimate the causal impact on operating performance, payout, leverage, and executive outcomes over the three years following the intervention.

Why appropriate?  
• Event studies are standard for testing whether new information (the 13D filing) conveys value-relevant news to shareholders. The precise revelation date, narrow window, and high-frequency CRSP data make the market-efficiency assumptions credible.  
• DiD exploits within-firm changes after activism and contrasts them to similar non-target firms, purging unobserved time-invariant firm heterogeneity (firm FE) and common macro shocks (year FE). The staggered adoption framework (Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021) handles multiple treatment years and avoids negative-weight problems.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
• Treated = 1 for firm i in fiscal year t if firm i’s first hedge-fund 13D filing date τ ∈ [t, t+1), i.e., τ occurs in or before year t and no earlier activism in the sample. Observation remains treated for all t ≥ τ (intent-to-treat).

Control group  
• Publicly traded U.S. firms that never receive hedge-fund activism during 2001–2006, plus as robustness firms that will be treated but have not yet been treated (“not-yet-treated” controls).

Treatment timing / event date  
• τ = trading day of first Schedule 13D (time 0).  
• Event study windows: [-10, +10] for announcement CARs; [-250, +250] for long-run BHARs.  
• DiD sample starts t = -3 fiscal years before τ and runs to t = +3, discarding ±1 fiscal-year overlaps when τ falls mid-fiscal year.

No RDD applies; no cutoff.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
Event Study  
E1. Semi-strong market efficiency: prices impound the expected NPV of activism within the short event window. Plausible for large U.S. equities and narrow windows.

DiD  
D1. Parallel pre-trends: absent activism, outcome paths of treated and control firms would have evolved similarly. Checkable with pre-treatment leads.  
D2. No differential anticipation: 13D filing is the first public signal; activists accumulate shares quietly, and SEC allows 10-day filing lag. Still, leakage risk exists but should be modest in yearly accounting data.  
D3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): activism in one firm does not change outcomes in controls. Industry-level contagion unlikely but we will cluster by 3-digit SIC and show robustness excluding firms in the same industry-year of a treated firm.  
D4. No time-varying selection on unobservables correlated with outcomes after conditioning on observables and FEs. Matching and rich controls mitigate this.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Self-selection of activists into firms with high latent improvement potential.  
   • Propensity-score / coarsened-exact matching on prior ROA, Tobin’s q, size, leverage, G-Index, past returns, and industry × year fixed effects.  
   • Include firm FE; use event-time leads to show similar pre-trends.

2. Concurrent shocks (M&A rumors, earnings surprises) driving both activism and outcomes.  
   • Drop observations where another major corporate event (merger proposal, CEO death, class-action filing) is reported in Factiva within ±30 days of τ.  
   • Control for firm-level news intensity; add event-specific controls (past-return decile, prior 13F hedge-fund ownership).

3. Treatment contamination / spillovers.  
   • Exclude potential peers in the same 3-digit SIC within the same calendar month for robustness.  
   • Cluster standard errors two-way: firm and calendar year.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# PACKAGES ----
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # FE regressions
library(estimatr)       # robust SEs
library(roll)           # rolling betas for market model
library(CBPS)           # propensity score weighting
library(did)            # Callaway & Sant’Anna DiD
library(tidyverse)

# 1. LOAD DATA ----
crsp   <- fread("crsp_daily.csv")        # PERMNO, date, ret, mktret
comp   <- fread("compustat_annual.csv")  # gvkey, fyear, roa, ebitda_sales,...
events <- fread("hedgefund_13d.csv")     # gvkey, permno, event_date, activist_id
controls <- fread("firm_controls.csv")   # inst_own, gindex, herf, execucomp vars

# 2. PREPARE EVENT STUDY ----
events <- events[, event_date := as.IDate(event_date)]
crsp   <- crsp[, date := as.IDate(date)]

# Market‐model abnormal returns
# Step 1: estimate firm-level beta on [−250,−30] before τ
get_car <- function(permno, ev_date){
  hist <- crsp[permno == !!permno & 
               date %between% c(ev_date - 250, ev_date - 30)]
  fit  <- lm(ret ~ mktret, data = hist)
  beta <- coef(fit)["mktret"]
  alpha<- coef(fit)["(Intercept)"]
  window <- crsp[permno == !!permno &
                 date %between% c(ev_date - 1, ev_date + 1)]
  window[, abn := ret - (alpha + beta * mktret)]
  return(sum(window$abn))
}
events[, car3 := mapply(get_car, permno, event_date)]

# 3. BUILD DID PANEL ----
# Merge all yearly data
panel <- comp[gvkey %in% events$gvkey | TRUE]   # keep treated + controls
panel <- merge(panel, controls, by = c("gvkey","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment indicator and event time
first_event <- events[, .(event_year = min(year(event_date))), by = gvkey]
panel <- merge(panel, first_event, by = "gvkey", all.x = TRUE)
panel[, treat := as.integer(!is.na(event_year) & fyear >= event_year)]
panel[, rel_year := fyear - event_year]   # event time

# 4. PROPENSITY WEIGHTS ----
pre <- panel[rel_year == -1]  # covariates one year before treatment
ps <- CBPS(treat ~ size + roa + q + leverage + gindex + pastret,
           data = pre, ATT = 1)
panel$w <- cbps.weights(ps)[match(panel$gvkey, pre$gvkey)]

# 5. MAIN DID (two-way FE, ATT weights) ----
did_mod <- feols(roa ~ i(rel_year, treat, ref = -1) | gvkey + fyear,
                 data = panel, weights = ~w, cluster = ~gvkey)
etable(did_mod, se.bonferroni = TRUE)

# 6. EVENT-STUDY STYLE COEFFICIENT PLOT ----
iplot(did_mod, ci = TRUE, ref.line = -1)

# 7. ROBUSTNESS: NOT-YET-TREATED CONTROLS VIA did PACKAGE ----
cs <- att_gt(yname = "roa",
             tname = "fyear",
             idname = "gvkey",
             gname = "event_year",
             xformla = ~ size + leverage + q + pastret + inst_own,
             data = panel,
             panel = TRUE,
             bstrap = TRUE, cband = TRUE)
aggte(cs, type = "dynamic") %>% summary()
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Based on prior literature and the incentives of hedge-fund activists:

Short-run CAR: +6 % to +8 % over the [-1,+1] window, statistically significant.  
Operating performance (ROA): +1.5 pp within three years (roughly 20 % of pre-event mean).  
Payout ratio: +5 pp; leverage: +2 pp; R&D spending: −0.3 pp; CEO turnover probability: +10 pp.  
I expect most of the shareholder gains to reflect genuine value creation rather than wealth transfers; bond spreads may widen modestly (≈10 bps), suggesting some redistribution from creditors.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends visually and statistically verified …… 0.8  
C2: No differential anticipation/leakage ………………………………………… 0.6  
C3: SUTVA / no spillovers ……………………………………………………………… 0.7  
C4: Properly handled staggered timing & weights ………………………… 0.9  
C5: Robust SEs & multiple robustness checks ……………………………… 0.9  
Overall average ≈ 0.78 → reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
